column3: Two measuring cups labeled 0.1 and 0.2, each secretly overfilled by a molecule at the factory (binary rounding): pour them together and the beaker needle trembles at 0.30000000000000004.
column4: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004 because 0.1 and 0.2 have no finite binary expansion - like 1/3 in decimal, rounded at parse time.
column6: Precision loss during math - the addition is fine; the inputs themselves were never exactly 0.1 and 0.2.

column3: A carpenter checks two beams with a feeler gauge instead of demanding atom-perfect flushness: gap thinner than the epsilon leaf means 'equal' - and he picks a thicker leaf for longer beams (relative tolerance).
column4: Never == floats: compare within tolerance, abs(a-b) <= max(rel*max(|a|,|b|), abs_tol), as math.isclose does.
column5: math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) -> True
column6: Fixed absolute epsilon - one absolute epsilon fails at huge or tiny magnitudes; combine with relative tolerance.

column3: A pizza cutter with two blades: the smooth wheel (/) slices fair fractional slivers; the guillotine blade (//) chops whole slices and sweeps the crumbs off the table, flooring toward minus infinity.
column4: Python / is always float and // floors; C's int / truncates toward zero - forgetting which yields surprise 0s or 3-instead-of-3.5.
column6: Truncation vs floor - C truncates toward zero (-7/2 == -3); Python floors (-7//2 == -4).

column3: Two carousel operators counting your backward laps: the Python operator always reports which painted horse (0, 1, 2) you stopped on - never negative; the C operator reports your overshoot, minus sign and all.
column4: Languages disagree on -7 % 3: Python gives 2 (sign of divisor, floored division); C/Java/JS give -1 (sign of dividend, truncated).
column6: Remainder vs modulo - truncated division yields a remainder with the dividend's sign; floored yields the divisor's sign.

column3: A masked ghost in a hall of mirrors that casts no reflection: hold NaN up to any mirror - even its own - and equality shows nothing (NaN != NaN); shake its hand and you turn ghost too (propagation).
column4: NaN ('not a number') results from invalid float ops (0/0, inf - inf), poisons all arithmetic, and is unequal to everything - even itself.
column5: float("nan") != float("nan") -> True / math.isnan(x) # the only honest test
column6: None/null - None means 'no value' and equals itself; NaN is a real float value that never equals anything.

column3: A bank teller's brass balance that weighs coins in powers of ten: every cent has its own labeled drawer, and the teller must sign a rounding policy before any drawer may be split.
column4: Decimal/BigDecimal store base-10 digits exactly with explicit rounding rules - mandatory for money; Fraction keeps exact ratios.
column5: from decimal import Decimal / Decimal("0.1") * 3 -> Decimal("0.3")
column6: Decimal(0.1) - constructing from the float smuggles in the binary error; always build from a string, Decimal("0.1").

column3: A hotel with 2^53 rooms: past the top floor, keys only come in even numbers - guest ...993 is silently checked into room ...992, and the JavaScript front desk never mentions it.
column4: Doubles represent integers exactly only up to 2^53; beyond that whole numbers round - JS's single Number type corrupts big IDs silently.
column5: JS: 9007199254740992 + 1 -> 9007199254740992 / Python ints stay exact at any size
column6: Integer overflow - overflow wraps fixed-width ints; here the float format skips odd integers past 2^53 without wrapping.

column3: A line worker yanks the red andon cord and hurls the defective part straight up through every floor of the factory; work halts on each floor it passes until someone's catcher's mitt snags it.
column4: An exception is an object thrown when an operation cannot proceed; it aborts normal flow and unwinds the stack until caught.
column5: raise ValueError("bad input")
column6: Error code - a returned code waits politely to be checked (and gets ignored); an exception forcibly interrupts flow.

column3: Firemen holding round canvas nets (except clauses) beneath a burning building (the try block): whatever leaps from the risky floors lands in the first net whose label matches its type.
column4: try wraps risky code; except/catch clauses receive matching thrown exceptions so the program can handle failure and continue.
column5: try: / x = int(s) / except ValueError: / x = 0
column6: finally - except runs only on a matching failure; finally runs on every exit path.

column3: A theater janitor who sweeps the stage after every show: hit performance, cancelled show, or the lead storming off mid-scene (an exception) - the broom always makes its pass before the doors lock.
column4: finally runs on every exit from try - success, caught or uncaught exception, even return - making it the home of cleanup.
column5: try: / f = open(p); work(f) / finally: / f.close()
column6: try/else - Python's else clause runs only when try succeeded; finally runs unconditionally.

column3: A family reunion where security arrests by surname: the warrant says 'anyone named LookupError' and both cousins KeyError and IndexError get cuffed. Arrest patriarch BaseException and you drag in even Ctrl-C.
column4: Exceptions form a class tree: a handler for a base class catches all subclasses, so order handlers specific-first.
column5: except LookupError: # catches KeyError and IndexError
column6: Exception vs BaseException - BaseException also covers KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit; catching it is almost always too broad.

column3: Airport customs: checked exceptions are checked luggage - declare every bag on the form (throws IOException) or the compiler refuses boarding; unchecked ones are pickpockets strolling through undeclared.
column4: Checked exceptions (Java) must be declared or handled at compile time; unchecked ones (RuntimeException, all of Python) fly free.
column5: Java: void read() throws IOException; / NullPointerException needs no throws clause
column6: Java Error - Error (OutOfMemory) is unchecked and unrecoverable by design; checked-ness is about compiler enforcement.

column3: Two restaurants: in the C diner the waiter slips a folded '-1' under your plate and hopes you notice before eating; in the exceptions bistro the chef bursts out and flips your whole table when a dish fails.
column4: Error codes return failure in-band for callers to test - and forget; exceptions use a separate channel that cannot be silently ignored.
column5: C: n = read(fd, buf, sz); // -1 on error / Go: val, err := f() / Python: raises OSError
column6: Result types - Rust's Result is explicit like codes but unignorable like exceptions, enforced by the type system.

column3: An avalanche investigator following boot prints back up the mountain: the deepest print is where the climber fell (the raising line); each print above names the ridge - file and line - that led there.
column4: A stack trace snapshots the call chain at throw time; read Python's bottom-up from the failing line through each caller.
column5: Traceback (most recent call last): / File "app.py", line 12, in main / ValueError: bad input
column6: Exception message - the message says what went wrong; the trace says where and via which call path.

column3: A fuse box that pops the instant one wire frays - lights out in one room - versus a house that stays lit while the wiring smolders in the walls, then burns down three suburbs from the fray.
column4: Detect bad state early and stop loudly at the source (asserts, validation) instead of limping on and corrupting data far from the cause.
column5: def withdraw(amount): / assert amount > 0, "negative amount"
column6: Graceful degradation - tolerance suits user-facing edges; fail fast suits internal invariants where continuing hides bugs.

column3: A pelican security guard gulping every alarm bird into its silent pouch - fire alarms, burglar alarms, the boss's Ctrl-C parrot - then smiling at the auditors: 'all quiet here.'
column4: except: pass hides real failures - even Ctrl-C; catch the narrowest type and at minimum log before continuing.
column5: try: risky() / except: pass # hides everything / except ValueError: log.warning(...) # better
column6: Intentional suppression - contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError) names exactly what is safely ignorable; bare except hides all.

column3: A relay runner catches a flaming baton, tapes a note to it - 'happened while loading config' - and hurls it onward; the tape ('from e') keeps the original scorch marks readable underneath.
column4: Bare 'raise' rethrows the current exception intact; 'raise New(...) from e' wraps it while preserving the original cause and traceback.
column5: except KeyError as e: / raise ConfigError("bad key") from e
column6: raise New() without from - Python shows an implicit 'During handling...' note; explicit from marks the true cause, from None hides it.

column3: Drinking a river through a straw: the water arrives in exactly the order the river sends it, you can't re-sip yesterday's gulp, and you never need a lake-sized cup.
column4: A stream is a sequential channel of data consumed piece by piece, in order, usually unrewindable, never needing to fit in memory.
column5: for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(8192), b""): / process(chunk)
column6: File - a file on disk is random-access and seekable; a stream is the sequential flow of reading or writing it.

column3: A short-order cook with a mouth-tube (0) delivering order slips, a serving hatch (1) sending dishes down the pipe to the next kitchen, and a side window (2) for shouting complaints at the manager - shouts never land on the plates.
column4: Every process gets stdin (fd 0), stdout (fd 1) for results, stderr (fd 2) for diagnostics - split so pipes carry data, not errors.
column5: cmd | sort # pipes stdout only / print(msg, file=sys.stderr)
column6: stdout vs stderr - both often hit the same terminal, but redirection splits them: 2> captures only errors.

column3: A cloakroom ticket from the OS's coat check: the numbered tag (descriptor) is your only way back to the coat, the attendant remembers where you left off, and the rack holds a limited number of tags before new customers are turned away.
column4: open() returns a file object wrapping an OS descriptor that tracks position and mode; descriptors are finite, so every open needs a close.
column5: f = open("log.txt", "a") / f.write(line) / f.close()
column6: Path - the path is the file's address; the handle is a live, stateful connection to the file.

column3: A submarine airlock: step in and the machinery arms itself; however you leave - walking out calmly or blown out by an explosion - the hatch slams and seals itself behind you.
column4: with open(...) as f guarantees close() on block exit - success or exception - via __enter__/__exit__; RAII's Python cousin.
column5: with open(p) as f: / data = f.read() # closed even on error
column6: try/finally - with is sugar for try/finally-close, minus the boilerplate you'd eventually forget.

column3: Two mail slots at a translator's office: the 'r' slot runs every letter through the resident interpreter (decoding, newline smoothing); the 'rb' slot drops the envelope on your desk unopened - the only safe slot for a shipped clockwork (a JPEG).
column4: Text mode ('r') decodes bytes to str and translates newlines; binary ('rb') yields raw bytes - required for images, zips, exact round-trips.
column5: open(p).read() # str / open(p, "rb").read() # bytes
column6: Windows newlines - text mode maps \r\n to \n; opening a JPEG in text mode corrupts it.

column3: A postal clerk piling your letters into a mailbag, driving to the depot only when the bag is full: your 'sent' love letter is still in the bag when the power dies - unless you yell FLUSH and he drives now.
column4: Writes sit in a memory buffer until it fills, the stream closes, or you flush() - so 'written' output may not be on disk or screen yet.
column5: print("working...", end="", flush=True) / f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
column6: flush vs fsync - flush empties the app buffer into the OS; fsync forces the OS cache onto physical disk.

column3: Two ways to eat spaghetti: the slurper inhales the entire bowl in one breath - fine until the bowl is 40 GB - while the twirler winds one fork-line at a time and never needs a bigger mouth.
column4: read() loads the whole file into memory; iterating the file object streams line by line in constant memory - choose by file size.
column5: data = f.read() # all at once / for line in f: # lazy, constant memory / handle(line)
column6: readlines() - readlines() still loads everything into a list; 'for line in f' is the lazy one.

column3: Two sets of directions to a house: the absolute deed reads from the planet's root ('/earth/usa/main-st/42'), while the relative sticky note ('two doors left') turns worthless the moment you - the CWD - wander to another street.
column4: Absolute paths start at the root; relative ones resolve against the current working directory - join with pathlib, never string +.
column5: from pathlib import Path / p = Path(base) / "data" / "a.csv" / p.resolve()
column6: CWD vs script dir - relative paths resolve from where the process launched, not where the .py lives; use Path(__file__).parent.

column3: A hotel's self-shredding notepad by the phone: each guest gets a page with an unguessable serial number so no two guests ever collide, and the page dissolves the moment they hang up (close).
column4: tempfile creates scratch files with unique names atomically - dodging collisions and predictable-name attacks - and can auto-delete on close.
column5: with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".csv") as f: / f.write(data)
column6: Hardcoded /tmp/foo - a fixed name invites collisions and symlink attacks; tempfile creates uniquely and atomically.

column3: Pulling rope from a well hand over hand until suddenly your fists close on air: no 'end knot' was ever tied - the empty grab itself is the message that the well is done.
column4: EOF is not a character - reads signal it by returning empty ('' or b'') in Python or -1 in C; loops must test for it to stop.
column5: while True: / chunk = f.read(4096) / if not chunk: break
column6: Ctrl-D / Ctrl-Z - those keystrokes make the terminal close stdin, causing EOF; they are not characters in the data.

column3: A spring-loaded cafeteria tray dispenser (stack): trays slap on and pop off in strict order, wiped instantly. Beside it sprawls a flea-market yard (heap) where objects squat at odd addresses until someone hauls them away.
column4: The stack holds each call's locals in LIFO frames freed automatically at return; the heap holds allocated objects with arbitrary lifetimes.
column5: def f(): / x = 1 # frame slot on stack / obj = MyClass() # object lives on heap
column6: Stack (data structure) - the call stack is a specific runtime memory region; the ADT is any LIFO container.

column3: A treasure map tattooed with pure coordinates: the map weighs nothing yet leads your shovel (*) straight to the chest - and adding 1 to the coordinates strides exactly one chest-width east (pointer arithmetic).
column4: A pointer is a variable holding a memory address; dereferencing (*p) follows it to the value, and arithmetic steps it through arrays.
column5: C: int x = 5; int *p = &x; / *p = 7; // x is now 7
column6: Reference - a reference is an opaque alias with no arithmetic or arbitrary addresses; pointers are raw and nullable.

column3: A hotel intercom labeled 'Suite 9': press it and you're simply talking to whoever occupies the suite - you never learn the street address and can't ask the intercom for 'the room next door'.
column4: A reference is a managed alias to an object - no visible address, no arithmetic, often non-null - the safe indirection of Java/Python.
column6: Pointer - pointers expose the address and allow arithmetic and null; references hide all of that.

column3: A photocopier bolted into the function's doorway: every argument walks up, a photocopy steps inside while the original waits in the lobby - scribble on the copy all you like.
column4: Pass by value copies the argument into the parameter, so reassigning the parameter never touches the caller's variable.
column6: Pass by object reference - Python copies the reference: rebinding the param does nothing, but mutating the shared object shows outside.

column3: Instead of a photocopy, the caller shoves their actual house key under the function's door on a string: the function unlocks the caller's own cupboard and rearranges it, and the changes are waiting when the caller gets home.
column4: Pass by reference aliases the caller's variable itself, so assigning the parameter rewrites the caller's variable (C++ &, C# ref).
column5: C++: void f(int &n) { n = 99; } / int x = 5; f(x); // x == 99
column6: Mutating a passed object - Python/Java can mutate shared objects but cannot rebind the caller's variable; true by-ref can.

column3: A night watchman in a museum follows every rope from the entrance (the roots), tagging each statue the ropes reach; at dawn, everything untagged is forklifted to the crusher - even beautiful statues no rope touches.
column4: A tracing GC walks references from roots (stack, globals) to find live objects and reclaims everything unreachable.
column5: obj = Big() / obj = None # unreachable -> collected eventually
column6: Reference counting - refcounting frees at zero instantly but leaks cycles; tracing GC handles cycles but must scan.

column3: Two shipwrecked sailors each gripping the other's life-rope: the rescue rule - 'haul out anyone no rope holds' - never fires, so the pair float in the ocean forever holding each other, until the cycle-cutter boat (gc) circles by with shears.
column4: Refcounting frees an object the instant its count hits zero, but mutual references never reach zero - CPython adds a cycle collector.
column5: a = {}; b = {"a": a}; a["b"] = b / del a, b # cycle: only gc reclaims it
column6: Tracing GC - tracing asks 'reachable from roots?' so cycles die naturally; refcounting only asks 'how many holders?'

column3: A bathtub whose drain is fouled by a growing hairball of forgotten keychains (a global cache holding everything it ever saw): the tap keeps running, nothing drains, and by evening the whole house's floor (RAM) is underwater.
column4: A leak is memory never reclaimed - lost pointers in C, or GC'd objects kept reachable by forgotten caches, listeners, and globals.
column5: cache = {} / def get(k): / cache[k] = load(k) # never evicted: leak
column6: Dangling pointer - a leak is memory held too long; a dangling pointer is memory used after it was freed.

column3: You still carry the key to apartment 4B, but the tower was imploded and a bakery built on the lot - yet your key still turns something, and you're now icing a stranger's wedding cake believing it's your bathtub.
column4: A dangling pointer targets memory already freed; using it reads garbage, corrupts the allocator, or hands attackers a write primitive.
column5: C: int *p = malloc(4); / free(p); / *p = 7; // use-after-free
column6: Null pointer - null crashes predictably at dereference; a dangling pointer 'works' on garbage and fails far from the bug.

column3: One actor working two shows under two stage names: shave 'Bob' bald for the matinee and 'Robert' walks on stage bald that evening - only hiring a body double (copy) gets you two heads of hair.
column4: Aliasing is two names bound to one object, so mutation through either shows through both; b = a copies nothing - use copy() to fork.
column5: a = [1]; b = a / b.append(2) # a -> [1, 2] / c = a.copy() # independent
column6: Shallow vs deep copy - a.copy() forks the outer list but inner objects stay aliased; deepcopy forks every level.
